Day 1, the festival lunch. An uncle started on the new tax slabs and Nandini answered sharply, and within a minute three people were talking at once. Her cousin Bhupen clapped his hands. "Carrom board! Losers wash the glasses!" The table laughed, and half of them moved to the veranda.

Day 3. The argument came back over breakfast. This time Bhupen handed Nandini a ball of dough and said, "You're on rotis, I'm on jokes." They both giggled.

Day 5. Nobody had changed their mind about the tax slabs. Nandini could still feel the knot about it. But the kitchen was noisy in a good way, and the carrom striker clicked all evening.

qa.q: What did Bhupen suggest on the first day when voices rose?
qa.a: Bhupen suggested a carrom board, with the losers washing the glasses.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling on Day 5, and what shows it?
qa.a: Nandini felt a lingering knot of frustration but also warmth, since the kitchen was noisy in a good way even though nothing was settled.

qa.q: What could Nandini do about the disagreement itself later, and why?
qa.a: Nandini could raise it another day in a quiet one-to-one talk, because the redirected evenings kept the peace but did not answer the question.

qa.q: How might the uncle who started on the tax slabs feel when Bhupen changes the activity?
qa.a: The uncle may feel a little cut off in the middle of a point, though also relieved that the mood lightened and nobody lost face.

passage:
Anjali, you want to know how our family survived all those election years without breaking apart? Sit. Your Bhupen dadu will tell you.
When I was twenty, every Bihu at our house in Jorhat ended the same way. My uncle and my elder brother would start on politics, and within half an hour the whole courtyard was shouting.
One year I decided to be the one who stopped it. Not by winning; by distracting. The moment voices went up, I clapped my hands and said, 'Enough parliament! Who's playing carrom? Loser washes the pitha plates!' My uncle laughed; he could never resist carrom. My brother went to help Ma in the kitchen, grumbling.
Did it fix anything? No. They disagreed until my uncle died. But every Bihu after that ended with carrom and laughter, not slammed doors.
So when your Mama and your Papa start at dinner tonight, Anjali, you know where the carrom board is.

qa.q: What did young Bhupen say when voices went up?
qa.a: 'Enough parliament! Who's playing carrom? Loser washes the pitha plates!'

qa.q: How did young Bhupen feel deciding to stop the fights?
qa.a: Determined to keep the festival warm, and light-hearted enough to use a joke instead of an argument.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what did it change?
qa.a: The year Bhupen chose to distract rather than argue; it did not end the disagreement, but it ended the slammed doors.

qa.q: How might Bhupen's uncle have felt when carrom was suggested?
qa.a: Relieved and amused, happy to leave the argument for a game he loved.

grounding: Shows a young cousin ending rising political arguments with a joke and a game of carrom, keeping festivals warm without settling the disagreement.

The power went off in the middle of Diwali dinner, and in the candlelight the argument got louder. Jaya's father and Damini's father had started on the election over the sweets, and now, with nothing else to look at, they were leaning across the table at each other.
Jaya caught her cousin Damini's eye. They had agreed on this in the afternoon.
Damini stood up. 'Emergency announcement,' she said in a newsreader voice. 'The electricity board has declared that anyone still discussing politics must wash all the dishes by candlelight.' Her father snorted. Jaya's mother laughed.
Then Jaya pulled the carrom board from under the sofa. 'Candle carrom. Chachu, you and Papa against Damini and me. Losers make tea.'
The fathers grumbled, then got competitive. By the time the power came back, they were arguing about whether a striker had touched the queen.
Nothing about the election was settled. But nobody left the table angry, and the evening stayed Diwali.

qa.q: What did the pretend announcement say?
qa.a: That anyone still discussing politics must wash all the dishes by candlelight.

qa.q: What might Jaya have been feeling when she caught Damini's eye?
qa.a: Tense about the rising argument, but ready and determined, since they had a plan.

qa.q: What else could Jaya and Damini try if carrom doesn't work next time?
qa.a: Suggest helping in the kitchen or a walk outside, keeping the change light and warm.

qa.q: How might the fathers have experienced the evening?
qa.a: They stopped fighting and got competitive over carrom, ending the evening laughing instead of angry.

grounding: Shows cousins redirecting a rising political argument with a joke and a game of carrom, keeping the evening warm though nothing is resolved.
